<meta>continues from previous page: ...the complete revealing of the truths of what was foretold by the symbols of the revealed laws regarding the Seal [of Prophets], and stripping them of the garments of forms entirely, is deferred from his time. It only appears in the genesis of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>the Comforter/Helper</gloss> and the manifestation of his specific sainthood.</meta>

If [the truth] is revealed, it is because the Seal-prophecy in its essence is in the most complete state within the genesis of Prophecy, such that <margin>he reached the station of...</margin> its <unclear>glory</unclear> <margin>its exaltation</margin> folded <margin>its excellence</margin> into its naming, and no forms remained upon it. For the Truth has subtle realities that manifest in, and the <unclear>remnant</unclear> of those realities is the beauty of those Truths. Therefore, the <term>Paraclete</term> said all the prophets and the <unclear>disclosing</unclear> <margin>from</margin> realities of their prophets, but some of those manifestations remained. So, your understanding is that the requirement of Prophecy is paused and entrusted to the revealing of <insert>to there</insert> the manifestations of his specific sainthood, in consideration of what is appropriate for the readiness of the time. There is no doubt that the lights of the <term>Kingdom</term> <gloss>Malakut</gloss> are descending without an end to the <unclear>perceivers</unclear>, <margin>no end of</margin> and there is no restriction in them. The ray of the Sacred spreads over the prepared, detached souls. The path of Truth opens for whoever knocks at its door, meaning that the door of God is open. For the Bestower of Knowledge, who is at the High Horizon, the One who is not miserly regarding the Unseen, therein flash meanings of a rank such that it is hidden from one who possesses discernment. As the Guardians of the brilliant, preserved light informed, its action in the language comes from "preservation" in the sense of seizing. The intended meaning here is a subtle hidden-ness from the world of the senses.

The extinguishing of lights is evanescent, not stable, and it follows a flashing light <margin>the overflowing of</margin> upon the soul on the night of the "sleeping of the <term>Nawwuj</term>" <gloss>the storm-winds</gloss>. This is in the language, the violent wind that uproots houses. The intended meaning here is the hardship leading to the rejection of bodily powers. This is not achieved except by the blowing of the winds of attraction from the Higher Ascent, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Glad tidings to whoever sends the winds as heralds before his mercy." And the easy [way] is in his hand, meaning the hour of its owner, meaning the owner of preservation, descending; and it is a <unclear>luminous</unclear> <term>nur</term> <gloss>light</gloss> from him, ascending from him as a form of that witnessing.

<summary>This passage continues the discussion of the Paraclete as the manifestation of the final and complete phase of prophecy, explaining how the truths of earlier prophetic symbols are revealed through the sainthood of the Seal of Prophets. It further describes the spiritual states of detachment and the descent of divine light as necessary for the unveiling of hidden realities.</summary>

<keywords>Paraclete, Seal of Prophets, Sainthood, Malakut, spiritual illumination, Divine Knowledge, unveiling</keywords>

According to Preller, *Mythology* I, p. 269, this would refer to the sun, which is hardly correct. According to the usual explanation, which has good support in line 10, <term>prēu katastilbōn selas</term> <gloss>shining with a gentle light</gloss>, this concerns the planet Mars, which, as is known, glows with a red light. 7. <term>aitheros heptaporois eni teiresin</term> <gloss>among the seven-pathed constellations of the aether</gloss> was already explained by Matthiae through Proclus, *Hymns* IV 7: "or whether you dwell in the aether above the rims of the seven circles." Bergk remarked that one cannot think of spheres before Anaximander. Yet, no one would likely place this hymn in Anaximander's time.

8. <term>tritatēs hyper antygos</term> <gloss>above the third rim</gloss> is explained by the just-cited passage of Proclus.

9. <term>klythi katastilbōn</term> <gloss>hear me, shining down</gloss> is supported by *Orphic Hymns* 3, 9; 27, 11; 33, 27. Hemsterhuys and Ilgen wrote <term>katastilpson</term> <gloss>shine down</gloss>. — <term>eutharseos</term> <gloss>courageous</gloss> in DM is an obvious improvement on the <term>euthaleos</term> <gloss>blooming</gloss> transmitted in E and some manuscripts of the Paris class, which usually has a short alpha, but which also occurs with a long alpha. Jacobs already wrote <term>euthylē</term> <gloss>thriving</gloss>, *Anth. Pal.* 9, 247.

10. <term>biotēt</term> <gloss>life</gloss>—perhaps <term>neotēta</term> <gloss>youth</gloss>? "The word <term>biotēs</term> <gloss>life</gloss> points to a very late time" (Bernhardy, *Greek Literature*³ II I p. 417).

16. Ares a bringer of peace? At the foundation lies the view, as A. Matthiae already recognized, that he who brings the injury can also heal it.

In this way, one might be able to know where you must perform <term>antispasis</term> <gloss>revulsion, the drawing of humors away from an affected area</gloss> and when you must perform <term>metocheuresis</term> <gloss>derivation, the drawing of humors toward an affected area</gloss>. <term>Antispasis</term> is, in fact, counter-evacuation. For example, if humors are flowing from some other part of the body into the thigh, I should immediately open a vein in the arm, and by pulling the humors to the opposite side, I will intercept the rising cause. Or, I will place cupping glasses at the breast so that, by warming it, I may make it be rubbed by hand, or I will constrict the joint of the hands with ligatures. <term>Metocheuresis</term> is the redirection of humors. When there is a deposit, I will remove blood by opening a vein from the sole or from the ankle, and by drawing it toward the suffering part, I will divert and purge the place and the <term>semen</term> <gloss>seed or fluid</gloss>. Just as I apply cupping glasses to the part that is suffering, I will warm both [sides] and rub them, and bind them with ligatures. 

If, therefore, the right side of the womb or the body is suffering, I will draw blood from the right arm or the right leg, striking the vein that is on the inside, or that which belongs specifically to the limb that is suffering. If, however, the left side is suffering, it is necessary to draw blood from the left arm or leg. Likewise, if the liver is lower down, I will take blood from the right arm. If the spleen, from the left, striking the interior vein. If some upper part of the body is suddenly afflicted, such as the throat of those with <term>cynanche</term>, or eyes that are hot or inflamed, or sudden pains, I will draw blood from those very same upper parts, whether by <term>antispasis</term> or by <term>metocheuresis</term>, and I will diligently apply purgatives, considering the reason and quality of these things, just as I will use an <term>elisterium</term> <gloss>clyster or enema</gloss> if the cause of the lifestyle requires it. If these are applied usefully and quickly at the beginning, [it is well]. If, however, the cause is <term>chronia</term> <gloss>chronic</gloss>, that is, already long-standing, then blood should be drawn more from the suffering place or limb itself. 

Thus, we also incise veins under the tongue of those with <term>cynanche</term>, as is said to evacuate the whole time, and nevertheless, for the cause of diet, [one must] persist for a long time. For the spleen and the liver themselves, we apply cupping glasses with a scalpel, and we purge any other place by scarifying, when the cause of the diet has already become chronic and no humor is flowing in it anymore. Otherwise, if it is done when it is not, I will not say it will be aided by fruits, but rather [it will be] greatly harmed. But above all, one must consider that we know the quality or virtue of the medicines and the nature of the places or limbs themselves that are suffering. For some of them feel [effects] slowly and endure the strength of medicines for a long time. Some feel it immediately and do not endure it for long. And because the limbs feel it quickly, they require more vehement and sharp applied benefits to be healed, if they are applied too harshly or beyond measure.

<summary>This passage details the medical techniques of antispasis (revulsion) and metocheuresis (derivation) used to manage the flow of humors in the body, emphasizing the importance of anatomical location and the duration of the ailment, whether acute or chronic, in determining the correct site for bloodletting and the use of cupping or scarification.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> and the healing process <note>original: "al-‘afwah"</note> is below it, or it is not positioned at the bottom. Likewise, the hand, the palm, and others always have the healing process oriented downward.

Thus, this is his statement. He says: Sometimes the wound occurs where it requires you to perform a complete amputation. As for the limb, if the wound has caused a large amount of tissue loss, it requires flesh-regenerating agents. It is not enough to use what dries and inhibits; rather, the drying and inhibiting agent sometimes blocks the material from which the flesh grows. The depression and loss in the bone may be such that it cannot fully regenerate, so a depression remains, as in a condition that may occur where more than the necessary amount grows, resulting in *proud flesh* <note>excessive granulation tissue</note>. The patient whose flesh one intends to regenerate in a wound must be monitored without this, for good regeneration may be such that it allows the flesh to grow. As for the skin, because if it has been completely severed, flesh grows in its place that is hard and upon which hair and veins do not grow, though branches form and it grows like flesh.

Among the wounds are dangerous wounds: the wounds that occur in the nerves and the muscles of the arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves, and the symptoms that follow them are abominable and bad. The worst of what follows a wound to the tip of the arm is a change in color and the disappearance of the pulse after it, followed by shrinkage, leading to fainting and a collapse of strength. Convulsions may also follow it. Likewise, those that occur in front of the knee at the kneecap, for they are followed by bad symptoms, and they are usually such that they rarely recover from them. And if a convulsion occurs from such brachial <note>arm-related</note> wounds and the treatment does not heal it, the treatment is the amputation of the arm, and God knows best.

<summary>This passage discusses the management of deep wounds, the necessity of flesh-regenerating agents versus drying agents, and the treatment of severe wounds involving nerves and muscles in the arm and knee.</summary>

# Number 6: Small Auspicious

<note>A woodblock illustration depicts a person sitting in a room, possibly consulting a priest or official, with a small table and screen.</note>

The house and grave are burdened by cause and effect,
Human relations are plagued by misunderstandings.
Guard against the loss of wealth and assets,
Only through prayer will you find balance.

▲ This oracle suggests you may be the target of personal resentment, or conversely, that you may be harmed by another, bringing misfortune upon yourself.
▲ In all matters, there are many errors, and there is a risk of losing wealth.
▲ Those who receive this lot should pray to the gods and Buddhas, rectify their hearts, and distance themselves from evil actions.
▲ You must exercise caution in all things.

<column-break/>

# Number 7: Great Bad Luck

<note>A woodblock illustration depicts a mountainous landscape with a figure walking along a path near a waterfall and trees.</note>

Boarding the boat, waiting for a favorable wind,
The moonlight is dim and hazy.
Wishing to travel far on the fragrant wheel <note>a metaphorical reference to a carriage or journey</note>,
High mountains stretch for thousands of layers.

▲ This lot is like boarding a boat and waiting for the wind; things will not go as you desire.
▲ Like moonlight hidden by clouds, your heart is confused and there is much agitation.
▲ Those who receive this lot must not act with impatience.
▲ In all matters, you must wait for the proper time.
▲ Pray to the gods and Buddhas to find peace of mind.
▲ The phrase "High mountains stretch for thousands of layers" signifies that there are many obstacles.

These are the words of Strabo: In Crete, the sacred rites of Jove are performed in a particular manner, accompanied by orgies. They called those youths who danced in armor Curetes. They also add a fable concerning the NATIVITY OF JOVE, saying that Saturn was accustomed to swallow his children as soon as they were born. Rhea, however, attempted to hide the pains of childbirth, to carry off the infant once brought forth, and to save him as much as possible. To this end, she used the aid of the Curetes, who, armed with tympana <note>kettledrums</note> and other instruments that produced a loud noise, danced with tumult around the Goddess; by this means, they frightened Saturn and deceived him while they carried away his son. By the same service, they nourished Jove after he was delivered to them. It is thought that they were called Curetes as if they were <term>curatores</term> <gloss>guardians</gloss>, either because they performed the <term>kourotrophian</term> <gloss>rearing of the child</gloss> of Jove, or because they served him. Suidas explains this when he asserts that the Curetes were the nurses and guardians of Jove.

Arnobius, in his work *Against the Gentiles*, book 3, commemorates those Curetes who are said to have hidden the wailing of Jove with bronze instruments, just as the Greeks indicate that the Samothracian fingers, five in number, are called the Idaean Dactyls. And elsewhere: Was Jove not saved from destruction by the benefit of the Curetes? They then carried him away into the hidden places of Mount Ida; hence, Crete is called the island of great Jove. Relevant to our subject is the commentary of Servius, in book 4 of the *Georgics*, page 149: Ops, the wife of Saturn, gave Jove to the Curetes, the Corybantes, and the Idaean Dactyls to be guarded on Mount Dictae in Crete, lest Saturn consume him, as he was accustomed to do with all his children.

> They report that the Dictaean Curetes once 
> Hid the wailing of that Jove in Crete,
> When the boys, in a swift dance around the boy,
> Armed, struck bronze against bronze in rhythm,
> Lest Saturn, having found him, send him to his jaws
> And deal an eternal wound to his mother under her breast.

These are the words of Lucretius, book 2. I will not pass over a very rare coin, dedicated to Antoninus Caracalla, celebrating DICTAEAN JOVE, minted by the Prasians, a people of Crete; concerning whom see Strabo, book 7, chapter 17, and the learned notes of Thomas de Pinedo, on Stephanus, under <term>PRAISOS</term>. The Deity sits holding a thunderbolt, around whom is read <term>ZEUS DIKTAIOS</term> <gloss>Dictaean Zeus</gloss>, and below, <term>PRASON</term> <gloss>of the Prasians</gloss>. The Cabiri were everywhere held to be most powerful. They were called <term>Apotropaioi Theoi</term> <gloss>averting gods</gloss>, <term>alexikakoi</term> <gloss>warders-off of evil</gloss>, <term>lysioi</term> <gloss>releasers</gloss>, <term>phyxioi</term> <gloss>putters-to-flight</gloss>, according to Julius Pollux: Gods who are envoys, repellers of evils, averters, solvers, and putters-to-flight of misfortunes. **S**Objection must also be made regarding these points concerning the nature of gold, which alone according to <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> is that in which no ailment appears. For neither part of its substance is infected or intemperate. Since it is composed, just as others are, of <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, its sulfur is most lucid and most clean, and by very strong washings it has been brought to a purity that has no combustible oiliness at all, nor any watery, phlegmatic humidity that can evaporate. It is perhaps sublimated and digested in concave places whose solid surface is often sublimated and digested by a temperate heat, in a digestion which is called <term>pepansis</term> <gloss>ripening</gloss>. And the earthy substance which is incorporated into the sulfur is clean and very subtle, suspended vaporously through the whole substance of the radical humidity of that sulfur itself. For this reason, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is complexional, departing in no way from the temperament, and this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances refined to the extremes. For the third thing, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not merely divided materially, but is most subtle vaporously, having been often sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the lifegiving heat of the sun and the stars. Similarly, the watery substance is also subtilized by the same method of repeated subtilization, and since it is thus present, it is subtilized finely. It is established that, when mixed together by the heat and the disposition of the place, which forces and reflects the vapor back upon itself, they are bound together by a very strong nexus of mixture. However, sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold merely by quality, but by substance, and because it is a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver and, by coagulating, it colors it. And since both have been led by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which arrive in the nature of transparency with a perpetual body, both will possess the fullness of purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will exist together. For this is a property of a subtle substance, that which stands through coagulation will have many parts in a very small space. Therefore, the contracted transparency will make a lemon-yellow color, and the subtlety makes the greatest <term>sfolidationem</term> <gloss>exfoliation/thinning</gloss>, and the constancy of many parts together in a small place and position creates weight, just as it is proven from those things that have been reasonably demonstrated in the *Physics* <note>referring to Aristotle's natural philosophy</note> and in the world. It remains, moreover, from the thinning and the temperament together, that gold is little evaporative or not at all, and therefore it is as if it is not odorous. Although an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong odor is nevertheless frequently accompanied by a smoky evaporation, for which reason it is further concluded that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and more resistant to fire because of its very strong mixture in the composition. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these things, one has the cause why certain things burn silver that do not burn gold, such as sulfur, arsenic, and certain others. The cause, therefore, of this-

<margin>Why gold is heavy.</margin>
<margin>Why gold does not burn.</margin>

<column-break/>

sort is the mixture, insofar as all of its earthy element is in the humidity, defending itself against burning, and all of its humidity is in the earthy element, restraining itself so that it does not fly away through evaporation, which connection <term>Plato</term> calls <term>fedus</term> <gloss>bond</gloss> and <term>Empedocles</term> the <term>glue of the elements</term>. From the temperament of gold, it is held why it is warm and moist, contributing to the trembling of the heart and to melancholy, which makes one sad. And because of this, it is also useful against the gold, to those things that make a man speak only to himself; it is useful against gold, if the passions or species of the same virtue are rubbed or even taken ground up. Because of its solidity, it is such that it does not stain the bodies it touches except with difficulty, and therefore it is worn in rings and other ornaments. Silver, however, stains a little, and other metals stain a lot, which the content does not touch, for the reason that the unctuous humor is separated in its entirety from them, to which the burnt earthy element is mixed in them, and this stains like the soot of an unctuous body. The great purity of the matter makes it so that it is very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but always as if it were a pure thing, which, when it is mixed with others, cannot retain such purity. And therefore it degenerates into copper. Conversely, it is very rarely found unless incorporated into stones. And this is why it is found as grains of sand frequently, because it is necessary that such purity be small and elevated from that matter and as if expelled, and therefore distinct; nevertheless, it is already found as a grain of <term>marchasita</term> <gloss>marcasite</gloss> together. # Absolution.

It is prohibited to confess sins sacramentally to an absent confessor via letters or a messenger, and to obtain absolution from the same absent party, under penalty of excommunication incurred automatically and reserved to the Roman Pontiff. No one is to defend, teach, print, or in any way put into practice such a proposition, even as one that might be considered probable in any case. Conversely, absolution from censures can indeed be conferred upon one who is absent, whether by letter, by messenger, or by another act that expresses the intention of the one absolving, as is evident from the rescripts and Bulls of Pontiffs directed to certain persons. The reason is that excommunication is an ecclesiastical penalty that can be inflicted even upon the absent, and therefore it can also be remitted.

13. The question arises: To whom should absolution be denied, and to whom should it be deferred?

Response: Judgment on this is left to the prudence of the confessor according to the circumstances that arise. However, it must be denied or deferred to those who are indisposed and who approach without having first examined their conscience; to those who lack the intention not to sin in the future; to those lacking supernatural contrition or attrition for their sins; to those unwilling to obey the confessor when he prescribes remedies to prevent them from relapsing; to those who are ignorant of the mysteries that are necessary by necessity of means; to those who are negligent in learning things necessary by necessity of precept; to those who do not make restitution when they are able to do so; to those who exist in the proximate occasion of sin, according to the points to be discussed under the heading *Proximate Occasion*; likewise, in any case or to those bound by a reserved excommunication; and finally, when there is no hope of amendment.
